title: From Usernames to People: What My First WikiConference India Taught Me
content:
A student contributor went to Kochi knowing the community through Gerrit and Phabricator. She came back wanting to build things with people.

I’ve been part of the Wikimedia community for about a year and a half. Most of that time, I knew it through a screen: Gerrit patches (code changes waiting for review), Phabricator tasks (where Wikimedia tracks its work), and a lot of refreshing the page to see if anyone had replied.

So when I landed in Kochi for WikiConference India 2026 Kochi(4–6 September), I was nervous. It was my first conference of this size. Looking back, it changed how I think about contributing.

Outside the community, I often get questions. “What do you actually do?” “What is Wikimedia?” At the conference, I could skip all that. I could mention Wikidata or a patch I was stuck on, and people just joined in.

Day 0 (3 September) was beneficial in this regard. There were introductions, an interactive session, and a celebration for the 25th anniversary of Creative Commons. By the time the main sessions started, I already felt a sense of belonging.

title: Growing Active Technical Contributors in ESEAP
content:
This article is a reflection on the author’s time in Wikimedia Indonesia from 2023-2026.

I joined Wikimedia Indonesia (WMID) in September 2023, during a transitional period. I was assigned to lead Wikidata programs in Indonesia, working with the Wikidata Indonesia Community. The learning curve was steep, but I was fascinated by how Wikidata describes real-world concepts, connects them, and the potential it holds.

Over time I met people from many backgrounds: academics, GLAM workers, activists, researchers working with data, students, and community members, and observed how they interacted with Wikidata. I saw a pattern: Wikidata is easier for people who already work with data, especially in computer-related fields.
snippet: This article is a reflection on the author’s time in Wikimedia Indonesia from 2023-2026.

title: Bringing Wikimedia to the Community: My Experience at the Festival Bahasa dan Budaya Dusun Sabah 2026 (FEBBEDS 2026)
content:
On 10 October 2026, I attended the Festival Bahasa dan Budaya Dusun Sabah at Dewan Masyarakat Ranau, Sabah. It was a great opportunity to celebrate Dusun language and culture, but for us as Wikimedians, it was also a chance to introduce Wikimedia projects to the local community and encourage more people to get involved in documenting their own culture.

During the festival, we set up a booth for Wikimedia Malaysia, where we introduced visitors to Wikimedia projects and explained how they could contribute to free knowledge. We managed to attract a few local visitors who were interested in learning more about what we do. It was encouraging to see people taking an interest in the projects and learning that there are different ways they can contribute, whether by sharing knowledge, taking photographs or documenting their culture.

title: From Milan to Toolforge: How a Wikimedia Hackathon Sparked WikiLinkua
content:
In May 2026, I travelled to Milan, Italy, for the Wikimedia Hackathon 2026. It was my first international trip, and an opportunity I had never imagined for myself. I arrived with a project idea, a few days to work on it, and no idea that I would leave with the beginnings of something I would continue building months later.

Looking back, Milan was not just about attending an international event. It was about discovering how a community of people with different backgrounds, skills, and interests can turn an idea into something others can use.

I arrived in Milan planning to work on a Wikidata watchlist filtering script. The idea was to make reviewing edits more manageable by allowing users to filter their watchlist by categories. I completed the script on the first day.

With time left, I joined an unconference session by Satdeep Gill and Silvia Gutiérrez. Their discussion introduced me to WikiLinkua, a language-learning platform built around Wikidata Lexemes and Wiktionary.

The idea caught my attention: what if people could learn a new language using languages they already know, while also helping improve the free knowledge that makes this possible?

title: From What We Explored at the September 2026 EduWiki Knowledge Showcase
content:
What can Wikimedia education look like in different learning environments?

The September 2026 EduWiki Knowledge Showcase brought together experiences from Wikimedia communities in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, giving participants an opportunity to hear how different education programmes are being developed and implemented in their communities. The session also included an update from the EduWiki Hub and a capstone project from the first cohort of the EduWiki Mentorship Program.

Mari Avetisyan of Wikimedia Armenia presented the organisation’s university internship programme, which gives students an opportunity to apply their academic knowledge and language skills through contributions to Wikimedia projects.

The internship runs for around two months. Students begin with Wikipedia training before creating articles, including translations from English, Russian, Chinese and Korean. Wikimedia Armenia currently works with three universities, and over eight years, 609 students have participated in the programme by contributing to Wikipedia.
snippet: What can Wikimedia education look like in different learning environments?

title: My experience at the Language Diversity Conference, Accra, Ghana
content:
Last week in Accra, I had the opportunity of being part of the maiden edition of the Language Diversity Conference held in Ghana, with the theme “Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Knowledge Movement”. I was one of the self-funded scholars, which Dagbani Wikimedians User Group funded to boost much participation in this conference.  The conference brought together over 82 language speakers and over 120 participants for a period of three days. It was hosted by the Dagbani Wikimedia User Group, Wikimedia UK, the Wikimedia Language Diversity Hub and Wikitongues.

This conference matters to all of us because digitalizing our languages goes a long way toward preserving them, and with them our pride. We have a lot of Dagaare speakers, and it would be unfortunate if we were unable to document our language. As Professor Samuel Alhassan Issah, Dean of the Faculty of Ghanaian Languages Education at the University of Education, Winneba, put it, “A language becomes minoritized because society makes it so, and even a language spoken by millions can be pushed to the margins.”

title: Can you guess today’s Wikipedia article in seven clues?
content:
Every day at midnight UTC, a new Wikipedia article goes into hiding. Your job is to find it.

WikiWhiz is a free daily guessing game I built on top of English Wikipedia and other sister projects. If you’ve played Wordle, the rhythm will feel familiar: one puzzle a day, same for everyone, and a result you can share with friends. The difference is the answer. Instead of a five-letter word, it is a Wikipedia article, and the clues come from the knowledge our communities have spent more than two decades building.

You start with one clue and a row of empty letter tiles showing the shape of the article’s title. There’s also a hint that tells you the number of words the answer has.

Type a guess into the tiles. Every guess must be the title of a real English Wikipedia article (random letters are not accepted). A wrong guess (or pass, if you can’t think of an answer) unlocks the next clue, up to seven in total. Each wrong guess also tells you two things:

  • How close the spelling is. A simple similarity score shows whether you are getting warmer or colder.

title: From Mentoring to Belonging: My Road to Wiki Journey as a Mentor – ROAD TO WIKI COHORT 2
content:
By Sarthak Singh, Mentor – Road to Wiki Cohort 1 & Cohort 2

When I first became a mentor for Road to Wiki, I thought my role would mainly involve helping people understand Wikimedia, Git, Gerrit, MediaWiki, and the process of making their first contribution. I soon realised that mentoring was about much more than teaching tools. It was about helping people find their place in the open-source community.

Across Cohort 1 and Cohort 2, I had the opportunity to interact with more than 200 people at different stages of their Wikimedia journeys. Some stayed until the end, some stepped away because of other commitments, and others returned after weeks of inactivity. A few went from asking how to get started to having their patches merged into real Wikimedia repositories. Watching that transformation has been one of the most rewarding parts of my own open-source journey.
snippet: By Sarthak Singh, Mentor – Road to Wiki Cohort 1 & Cohort 2

title: Leaves from The Story of My Journey to Kaohsiung
content:
I had the opportunity to attend the ESEAP Conference in May 2026 as a scholar. It was my first in-person meeting with colleagues and friends from the ESEAP Wikimedia Hub, and my second overseas experience with the global Wikimedia movement after the 2025 GLAM Wiki Conference in Lisbon. I arrived with one question: how can our communities grow technical contributions, from MediaWiki and templates to Wikidata reuse?

I landed on Thursday, 14 May, and promptly spent 45 minutes in immigration, the first time I had ever been detained. My papers were complete, including my E-TAC (Taiwan’s online arrival permit, which I used on the strength of my past Schengen visa). The real problem was the faded Portuguese entry and exit stamps, which the officers could not read until someone brought out a magnifying glass. Lesson learned: ask officers to press firmly when stamping. At the time I was sure I would be deported. Now I smile while remembering it.

Then I stepped outside, and the Kaohsiung sun and wind hit my face. It was stinging hot, exactly like Jakarta or Surabaya at midday. Pulling my suitcase, I smiled. It felt like home.

title: Three Days of Learning, Collaboration and Editing for Electoral Integrity
content:
From 28 to 30 September 2026, I participated in the Interactive Media Seminar for Electoral Integrity in Abuja, Nigeria. Organised by FIAP through FactCheckAfrica, in collaboration with Wikimedia User Group Nigeria, the seminar brought together Wikimedia editors, journalists, newsroom editors and fact-checkers to explore how reliable information can be documented and made accessible ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.

For me, the three days were an opportunity to learn, exchange ideas and put Wikimedia’s editorial principles into practice. I came away with a better understanding of how the work of journalists, fact-checkers and Wikimedia contributors can complement one another in addressing misinformation and disinformation.

The first day focused on Wikipedia’s approach to reliable information and the principles that guide its content. We discussed verifiability, reliable sourcing, neutral point of view and the prohibition against original research. We also explored how transparency and community participation help maintain the quality of Wikipedia articles.

title: From First Commits to Graduation: Reflecting on 8 Months at Road to Wiki Cohort 2!
content:
Celebrating growth, community, open-source impact, and high-octane memories in Gurugram!

Dates: 2 and 3 October 2026
Event: Graduation Day for Road to Wiki Cohort 2

Eight months ago, an ambitious group of developers set off on a journey into the world of open source. Organized by WikiClub Tech India and Open Knowledge India (OKI) at IIIT Hyderabad, out of over 200+ applicants who filled out the form, 50 developers embarked on this journey to become core open-source contributors.

Stepping into the role of Dev-Circle Lead meant working directly with student developers facing real-world engineering challenges. Navigating large-scale open-source ecosystems can feel daunting initially, so our focus was turning confusion into momentum.

  • Tackling Setup Blockers: We spent late nights working through environment issues, matching Node.js versions, configuring SSH keys, learning Gerrit code review rules, and setting up git commit hooks.
  • First Merges Across Wikimedia: Watching mentees land their first code merge was a high point of the program. Together, we contributed across several major projects, including MediaWiki core, MinervaNeue, GrowthExperiments, ProofreadPage, and Wikispeech.

title: Wikimedia Foundation Bulletin 2026 Issue 19
content:
Here is a quick overview of highlights from the Wikimedia Foundation since our last issue on September 25. Previous editions of this bulletin are on Meta. Let foundationbulletin@wikimedia.org know if you have any feedback or suggestions for improvement!

  • Community Wishlist: Community Wishlist is looking for volunteers to join their working group. You can find details on the goal of the group, roles and expectations, norms we’ll follow, and how to sign up on this Meta-Wiki page.
  • Human knowledge at stake: Wikimedia Foundation makes the case for human knowledge at the UN General Assembly and how scrapers are straining our infrastructure and the larger human knowledge ecosystem online.
  • Joy of contributing: How a simple thanks fuelled one of our Wikimedians of the Year as they connect the community.
  • PTAC technical topics: The Product and Technology Advisory Council calls for the community to suggest topics that it should consider and discuss with the Wikimedia Foundation. Submit your topic on the council’s talk page.
